analysis.one_liner: Stops credit card and loan companies from forcing customers to give up their day in court through fine-print arbitration clauses.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: no hearing, no vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal arbitration law to say that the fine print in a consumer credit contract — a credit card agreement, a loan for personal use — cannot force a borrower to give up their day in court before a dispute even happens. If a dispute later arose, the borrower and lender could still agree to arbitrate voluntarily. The bill was introduced by Senator Feingold with Senator Leahy in February 2000 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it received no hearings, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who borrow money for personal, family, or household purposes — credit card holders, auto loan borrowers, and similar consumers. Today, the fine print in these contracts usually requires any dispute to go to private arbitration, where a lender picks the forum, normal court rules do not apply, and appeals are nearly impossible. The bill would make those pre-written arbitration clauses unenforceable, so a consumer could take a billing error, a collection dispute, or an unfair charge to a real court. Consumers could still agree to arbitration voluntarily after a dispute actually arises.

how_it_helps.text: Under the Federal Arbitration Act, nearly every credit card and consumer loan contract today contains a clause requiring disputes to be settled by private arbitration rather than court. The bill would amend the federal arbitration law to make those pre-dispute clauses unenforceable in consumer credit contracts.

The bill is narrow on purpose: it leaves arbitration fully available when the consumer and lender agree to it after a dispute has already arisen, so it targets only contracts signed before the customer knows there is a problem.
It defines 'consumer credit transaction' to cover credit intended primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, the debt ordinary households take on.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders, credit card issuers, and other companies that lend money for personal, family, or household purposes would bear the cost. They could no longer force customers to sign away their right to go to court before a dispute happens, so they would face more disputes in court, including as part of class actions, and could no longer rely on a private arbitration process that lenders typically choose and pay for. Arbitration firms that earn fees handling credit disputes would lose that business. Lenders would likely try to pass some added costs on to borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is not always worse for consumers: it can be faster and cheaper than court for individual disputes, and lenders argue that removing arbitration raises their costs, which could show up in higher rates or fees for all borrowers.

The bill stops pre-dispute arbitration clauses but does nothing about the class-action waivers that often sit next to them in the same fine print, so some consumers could end up in court with no practical way to band together on small-dollar claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to millions of households that take on consumer debt and today sign away their court rights without realizing it; the cost falls on lenders, who would handle more disputes in court and might pass some of that on in pricing. Weighing that, the trade is favorable to ordinary borrowers: a lender-chosen private forum with no appeal is a poor substitute for court when the dispute involves a company that writes the rules of the contract. The bill's voluntary post-dispute carve-out is a sensible guard against the objection that arbitration is sometimes faster and cheaper. The bigger weakness is that the bill is narrow — it does not touch class-action waivers — but narrow scope is not a reason the bill failed; it died without a hearing, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2000 and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 29, 2000 by Senator Feingold with Senator Leahy, and read twice before being referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no Senate floor action after the referral.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died at the referral stage and had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers are better off because the bill died: they keep the fine-print clauses that route disputes into lender-chosen private arbitration instead of court. Arbitration providers that earn fees from those cases also keep the business.

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and spoke for it on the floor.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsor; introduced with Feingold.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill stayed there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held; the bill's two Senate supporters were both Democrats, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: These companies' standard contracts require disputes to go to arbitration forums that they choose and pay for, a process where consumers rarely win big and cannot appeal. Blocking the bill preserved that advantage.
Arbitration providers earn fees handling credit disputes under lender-chosen clauses; the bill would have eliminated most of that stream. Its defeat kept it intact.
